stem: An adult client with obesity and no diabetes is prescribed Wegovy (semaglutide) as part of a weight-management plan. The client says, “I thought semaglutide was only a diabetes medication.” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: Wegovy is an FDA-approved semaglutide product for reducing excess body weight and maintaining weight reduction long term in eligible adults when used with reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.
options.B: Semaglutide is approved only for type 2 diabetes, so using Wegovy for obesity is necessarily off-label.
options.C: All semaglutide products have identical FDA indications, so the product name and formulation do not matter.
options.D: Wegovy is used to treat acute hypoglycemia in adults who do not have diabetes.

rationale: A is correct. The current Wegovy prescribing information identifies semaglutide as a GLP-1 receptor agonist and includes reduction of excess body weight and long-term maintenance of weight reduction among its FDA-approved indications for eligible adults, in combination with reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. B is incorrect because Wegovy has FDA-approved non-diabetes indications. C is incorrect because semaglutide products are labeled for different indications and are not simply interchangeable on the basis that they contain the same active drug; for example, Ozempic is labeled for adults with type 2 diabetes and specific cardiovascular and kidney-risk indications. D is incorrect because semaglutide is not an acute treatment for hypoglycemia.
educational_objective: Distinguish FDA-approved indications among semaglutide products and recognize Wegovy as an approved option for long-term weight reduction in eligible adults rather than assuming semaglutide is used only for diabetes.
source_organization: U.S. National Library of Medicine DailyMed / U.S. Food and Drug Administration
source_document_title: WEGOVY (semaglutide) Prescribing Information; OZEMPIC (semaglutide) Prescribing Information
source_version_date: Current Wegovy label with major changes through June 2026; current Ozempic label with indication changes through January 2025 and safety updates through 2025; accessed 2026-08-17

OZEMPIC, Section 1 — type 2 diabetes glycemic-control, cardiovascular-risk, and chronic-kidney-disease risk indications
source_claim_supported: Wegovy and Ozempic contain semaglutide but have distinct FDA-labeled indications; current Wegovy labeling includes long-term weight reduction/maintenance for eligible adults, so semaglutide is not restricted to diabetes treatment.

audit_findings.clinical_category: GLP-1 receptor agonist pharmacology / semaglutide indications
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified directly against current DailyMed FDA labeling. The Wegovy label has major 2025–2026 indication/formulation updates, including weight reduction/maintenance, cardiovascular risk reduction, and MASH treatment for the injection formulation; Ozempic has separate diabetes/CV/CKD indications. The original broad source statement was therefore narrowed to a product-specific label claim.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: The final stem specifies Wegovy and obesity, making A directly label-supported without requiring an exact dose or implying that every semaglutide formulation has the same indication. The answer does not state that all adults with obesity are automatically candidates; it uses ‘eligible adults.’
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct. It accurately states the current FDA-labeled weight-management role of Wegovy.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect. Wegovy has FDA-approved indications beyond diabetes.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect. Semaglutide-containing products have distinct labeling and are not interchangeable solely because the active ingredient is the same.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect. Semaglutide does not serve as emergency treatment for hypoglycemia.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A accurately answers the client’s misconception while remaining product-specific. No alternative is defensible under current labeling.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are medication-indication statements of similar scope; the correct answer is not keyed by excessive numeric detail or brand familiarity alone.
audit_findings.blueprint: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies is directly appropriate because the nurse is teaching an FDA-labeled medication indication and distinguishing products containing the same active drug.
